Conic optimization

Source: vignettes/conic.Rmd
conic.Rmd
library(optcompR)

A conic program minimizes a linear (or convex quadratic) objective over the intersection of an affine set with convex cones. Many convex problems that are not linear or quadratic have exact conic forms: Euclidean norms, geometric means, matrix eigenvalues, entropy and log-sum-exp. optcompR supports four cones:

Function Cone Constraint
opt_soc_constraint(m, x, t) second-order \|x\|_2 \le t
opt_exp_cone(m, x, y, z) exponential y e^{x/y} \le z,\ y > 0
opt_pow_cone(m, x, y, z, alpha) power x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha} \ge |z|,\ x, y \ge 0
opt_psd_constraint(m, M) semidefinite M \succeq 0

Every argument must be affine in the decision variables once parameters are substituted. A model with cones is classified as "SOCP" when all its cones are second-order cones and as "CONIC" otherwise. Cones are convex sets, so the model is convex when its objective is linear or a convex quadratic and its rows are linear; that is recorded in the classification evidence.

Conic models are solved by Clarabel, an interior point solver available from CRAN as the clarabel package. SCIP also accepts second-order cones, which optcompR passes as the equivalent quadratic rows \|x\|_2^2 \le t^2,\ t \ge 0; that path also handles mixed-integer second-order cone programs ("MISOCP"). A solver that does not support a cone type is refused with a message naming the cone.

Second-order cones

The distance from the origin to the line x_1 + x_2 = 2 is \sqrt{2}. Minimize an epigraph variable t with \|x\|_2 \le t:

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2)
t <- opt_variable(m, "t")
line <- opt_constraint(m, sum(x) == 2, name = "line")
opt_soc_constraint(m, x, t)
opt_objective(m, t)
opt_classify(m)
#> <opt_classification: SOCP, convex>
#>   - syntactic: objective is linear; constraint rows: linear = 1
#>   - structural: 1 cone constraint(s) of type soc; cones are convex sets
#>   - structural: linear objective
r <- opt_solve(m)
r$solver
#> [1] "clarabel"
opt_objective_value(r)
#> [1] 1.414214
opt_value(r, x)
#> [1] 1 1

Row duals are shadow prices in the usual optcompR convention, \partial f^* / \partial b. Here f^*(b) = b / \sqrt{2}, so the dual of line is 1/\sqrt{2}:

opt_dual(r, line)
#>      line 
#> 0.7071068
1 / sqrt(2)
#> [1] 0.7071068

opt_check() verifies rows, bounds and cones at the returned point. The cone residuals appear in special. The KKT check is skipped for conic models because their multipliers live in the dual cones rather than on rows.

d <- opt_check(r)
d
#> <opt_diagnostics: feasible>
#>   max row violation (scaled):   6.21725e-15
#>   max bound violation (scaled): 0
#>   max integrality violation:    0
#>   max cone/indicator/SOS violation: 4.93957e-09
#>   objective recomputation error: 0
d$special
#>   constraint     kind    violation
#> 1      cone1 cone soc 4.939575e-09

A robust least squares fit

Second-order cones express norms of affine residuals. Minimizing \|Ax - b\|_2 exactly:

set.seed(3)
A <- matrix(rnorm(40), 20)
b <- A %*% c(1, -2) + rnorm(20, sd = 0.1)
m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2)
t <- opt_variable(m, "t")
opt_soc_constraint(m, A %*% x - b, t)
opt_objective(m, t)
r <- opt_solve(m)
opt_value(r, x)
#> [1]  1.018269 -1.993609
qr.solve(A, b)
#>           [,1]
#> [1,]  1.018269
#> [2,] -1.993609

The norm of the residual (not its square) is the objective, so the same solution as ordinary least squares comes out, and the norm itself can now be bounded, weighted or combined with other norms in one model.

Semidefinite cones

opt_psd_constraint() takes a square affine matrix expression. Only its upper triangle is used, so the matrix must be symmetric by construction. opt_sym_variable() creates a symmetric matrix of decision variables with k(k+1)/2 underlying variables.

The largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix A is the smallest t with tI - A \succeq 0:

A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 0,
              1, 3, 1,
              0, 1, 1), 3)
m <- opt_model()
X <- opt_sym_variable(m, "X", 3)
t <- opt_variable(m, "t")
opt_constraint(m, X == t * diag(3) - A)
opt_psd_constraint(m, X)
opt_objective(m, t)
opt_objective_value(opt_solve(m))
#> [1] 3.879385
max(eigen(A)$values)
#> [1] 3.879385

A matrix built from expressions works too. The matrix \begin{pmatrix}1 & x & 0\\ x & 1 & y\\ 0 & y & 1\end{pmatrix} is positive semidefinite exactly when x^2 + y^2 \le 1, so maximizing x + y gives \sqrt 2:

m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x")
y <- opt_variable(m, "y")
one <- 0 * x + 1
zero <- 0 * x
E <- c(one, x, zero, x, one, y, zero, y, one)
dim(E) <- c(3, 3)
opt_psd_constraint(m, E)
opt_objective(m, x + y)
opt_objective_value(opt_solve(m))
#> [1] 1.414214

Exponential cones

The exponential cone expresses e^x \le t, \log, entropy and log-sum-exp. Minimizing t subject to e^x \le t and x \ge 1 gives e:

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", lower = 1)
t <- opt_variable(m, "t")
opt_exp_cone(m, x, 0 * x + 1, t)
opt_objective(m, t)
opt_objective_value(opt_solve(m))
#> [1] 2.718282
exp(1)
#> [1] 2.718282

Log-sum-exp \log \sum_i e^{a_i^\top x} \le s is the set of points with \sum_i u_i \le 1 and e^{a_i^\top x - s} \le u_i, one exponential cone per term:

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x")
s <- opt_variable(m, "s")
u <- opt_variable(m, "u", dim = 3)
a <- c(1, -1, 0.5)
for (i in 1:3) opt_exp_cone(m, a[i] * x - s, 0 * x + 1, u[i])
opt_constraint(m, sum(u) <= 1)
opt_objective(m, s)
r <- opt_solve(m)
c(x = opt_value(r, x), lse = opt_objective_value(r))
#>          x        lse 
#> -0.2219656  1.0799137
f <- function(x) log(sum(exp(a * x)))
optimize(f, c(-5, 5))
#> $minimum
#> [1] -0.2219163
#> 
#> $objective
#> [1] 1.079914

Power cones

The power cone with exponent \alpha bounds a weighted geometric mean. With x + y \le 2, the largest z with x^{0.3} y^{0.7} \ge |z| is 2 \cdot 0.3^{0.3} 0.7^{0.7}:

m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x")
y <- opt_variable(m, "y")
z <- opt_variable(m, "z")
opt_constraint(m, x + y <= 2)
opt_pow_cone(m, x, y, z, alpha = 0.3)
opt_objective(m, z)
opt_objective_value(opt_solve(m))
#> [1] 1.085763
2 * 0.3^0.3 * 0.7^0.7
#> [1] 1.085763

Mixed-integer second-order cones

With integer variables and only second-order cones the class is "MISOCP", which SCIP solves to global optimality:

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, type = "integer", lower = -5, upper = 5)
t <- opt_variable(m, "t")
opt_soc_constraint(m, x - c(1.4, 2.6), t)
opt_objective(m, t)
opt_classify(m)$class
#> [1] "MISOCP"
r <- opt_solve(m)
opt_value(r, x)
#> [1] 1 3
opt_objective_value(r)
#> [1] 0.5656854

Accuracy

Interior point solvers stop at a relative tolerance near 10^{-8}. The status "almost_optimal" means Clarabel stopped at a reduced accuracy; check such points with opt_check() before relying on them. The reported bound is Clarabel’s dual objective, so opt_objective_bound(r) and the objective together bracket the optimum.
